question: What PFD carriage requirement applies to every vessel operating in Florida, regardless of length?
choice_a: PFDs are only required for children under 12
choice_b: Only the operator needs a PFD aboard
choice_c: One wearable USCG-approved personal flotation device of appropriate size for each person aboard, in serviceable condition and readily accessible
choice_d: No PFD is required if the boat has enough seating for everyone aboard
explanation: Federal and Florida law require a wearable, properly sized, serviceable, and readily accessible USCG-approved PFD for every person on board any vessel.

question: What additional PFD is required on vessels 16 feet or longer (except canoes and kayaks)?
choice_a: A second wearable PFD for every person already counted
choice_b: No additional device is required beyond wearable PFDs
choice_c: A Type V PFD for the operator only
choice_d: At least one USCG-approved throwable Type IV device that is immediately available
explanation: Vessels 16 feet and longer, other than canoes and kayaks, must also carry at least one throwable Type IV device (such as a ring buoy or buoyant cushion) immediately available for someone who falls overboard.
source_note: FWC PFD requirements by vessel length

question: Under Florida law, what must a child under 6 years of age wear while aboard a vessel less than 26 feet in length that is underway?
choice_a: A USCG-approved Type I, II, or III PFD
choice_b: No PFD is required for children under 6
choice_c: Only water wings or an inflatable pool toy
choice_d: A PFD only if the child cannot swim
explanation: Florida requires children under age 6 to wear a USCG-approved Type I, II, or III PFD while aboard a vessel less than 26 feet in length whenever the vessel is underway.

question: What does 'underway' mean for purposes of Florida's child PFD law?
choice_b: Anytime the vessel is not anchored, moored, made fast to the shore, or aground
choice_c: Only when the vessel is traveling faster than idle speed
choice_d: Only when the vessel is offshore, beyond sight of land
explanation: A vessel is considered underway anytime it is not anchored, moored, tied to shore, or aground, which is the trigger condition for Florida's under-6 PFD-wear requirement.

question: What PFD type is generally the most buoyant and best for offshore or rough-water use, though bulkier?
explanation: Type I offshore life jackets provide the most buoyancy and are designed to turn most unconscious wearers face-up, making them best suited for rough or remote water, though they are bulkier than a Type III.

question: Which PFD type is most commonly worn for general recreational boating and watersports because it is comfortable and allows freedom of movement?
explanation: Type III flotation aids are the most popular choice for general boating, fishing, and watersports because they are comfortable and allow good freedom of movement, though they do not reliably turn an unconscious wearer face-up.

question: What is a Type V PFD?
choice_a: A special-use device (such as an inflatable belt pack or work vest) approved only for the specific activity stated on its label
choice_b: A generic PFD usable interchangeably for any activity
choice_c: A device that never needs to be worn to count toward the carriage requirement
choice_d: A device used only on PWCs
explanation: A Type V PFD is a special-use device, such as an inflatable belt pack, deck suit, or work vest, that is USCG-approved only for the particular activity or conditions specified on its label; most must be worn (not just carried) to count toward the legal requirement.
source_note: USCG PFD type classifications, Type V restrictions

question: What condition disqualifies a PFD from satisfying Florida's carriage requirement even though it is the correct type?
choice_b: It is torn, waterlogged, deteriorated, or otherwise not in serviceable condition
choice_c: It is a bright color such as orange
choice_d: It was manufactured more than one year ago
explanation: A PFD must be in good, serviceable condition; a torn, waterlogged, or deteriorated PFD does not satisfy the legal requirement even if it is nominally the right type and size.

question: Why should PFDs be sized to the individual wearer rather than 'one size fits all'?
choice_a: All USCG-approved PFDs are automatically one universal size
choice_b: Sizing is a comfort preference with no safety consequence
choice_c: A PFD that is too large can slip off in the water, and one that is too small will not provide adequate buoyancy or fit
choice_d: Sizing only matters for adults, never for children
explanation: An oversized PFD can ride up and slip off an unconscious or panicked wearer, while an undersized one may not provide sufficient buoyancy, which is why PFDs are labeled by weight range and must fit the intended wearer.

question: Are inflatable PFDs approved for use by children or non-swimmers in Florida?
choice_a: Yes, inflatable PFDs are approved and preferred for young children
choice_b: Inflatable PFDs may be used by anyone regardless of age or swimming ability
choice_c: Inflatable PFDs are banned outright in Florida
choice_d: No -- most inflatable PFDs are approved only for those 16 and older and are not recommended for non-swimmers
explanation: Most inflatable PFDs are approved only for persons 16 years of age or older and are not recommended for non-swimmers, since they require the wearer to manually or automatically trigger inflation.

question: Why does Florida emphasize wearing a PFD at all times on the water rather than simply having one aboard?
choice_a: Most boating fatalities are drownings, and most victims were not wearing a PFD at the time of the accident, and falls and capsizings often happen too quickly to put one on afterward
choice_b: Wearing a PFD is only a suggestion with no safety benefit
choice_c: Florida law requires PFDs only be worn while docked
choice_d: PFDs are equally effective whether worn or simply stowed nearby
explanation: National boating fatality statistics consistently show drowning as the leading cause of death and that most victims were not wearing a PFD, since capsizing or falling overboard often happens with no time to put one on.
source_note: U.S. Coast Guard national recreational boating statistics
